models.section: 3.1 Search and matching under two currencies
models.summary: An extension of the Diamond-Mortensen-Pissarides search model to a market where legal tender and a digital currency circulate together. Fisher's equation prices the digital currency and Keynes's speculative demand explains its swings: velocity is fixed by the technology, so the price falls as more goods are settled in it and rises when speculative demand surges, and the risk is largest when few accept it. In a one-period closed market nobody holds both currencies. Buyers and sellers match at random, the match probability is the ratio of goods kinds, and the value of holding nothing, legal tender or digital currency satisfies three Bellman equations with storage costs and a discount rate. Sellers accept a currency exactly when holding it beats holding nothing plus the production cost. Each currency then has a threshold acceptance. At equilibrium one currency can sit at full acceptance while the other holds steady, so the two can coexist; if the second falls below its threshold it spirals out, and if it sits above it oscillates until it balances. Because digital storage is cheap, its threshold is low. Zimbabwe, which has already dropped its own currency, anchors the legal-tender threshold, and the United States, birthplace of many digital currencies, anchors the digital one. Acceptance probabilities for 130 countries are computed from real parameters and checked by an OLS regression on 53 countries, R-squared 0.282.

models.summary: The government maximizes the discounted sum of tax revenue. Digital adoption raises recognition, which raises output and the tax base, but it also shifts the base from legal tender to digital currency and adds supervision costs, concealment and the loss of macro control. Current revenue taxes each currency's matched trades at its own rate and subtracts a cost that grows with digital acceptance. Because willingness to switch payment methods moves slowly, the rates can only be optimized over time, so the government picks a pair of rates each period to nudge the mix until the present value of revenue net of supervision and risk is largest.

models.summary: Following Bacchetta and van Wincoop, an exporter's profit is written when the price is set in the exporter's currency and when it is set in the importer's, with the exchange rate random and normal. The gap in expected profit is proportional to the variance times the curvature of profit, so both sides pick the exporter's currency when profit is convex in the rate. Adding the digital currency as a third unit, the same comparison says it wins whenever its rate against the importer swings less than the rate between the two countries. Controlling its risk is therefore enough to make it the settlement currency of trade.
models.purpose: Show when the digital currency becomes the trade settlement unit.

models.summary: A two-track system keeps both a supranational digital currency and national currencies, against the textbook optimal-currency-area advice to drop the national ones. A world body issues the digital currency, allocates it to central banks in proportion to demand, and each central bank issues it onward. Its cross-country rate is fixed at one and its velocity is uniform. Supply follows estimated world output through Fisher, and the body targets inflation inside 1.5 to 2.5 percent, setting the nominal rate from the real rate plus the target. It also adjusts each country's supply by a weighted trade gap and capital gap, cutting supply when a deficit comes with capital inflow. National central banks keep an independent policy and a floating rate against the digital currency, given by purchasing-power parity, and capital runs to where the real rate is higher. A Monte Carlo simulation of US trade from 1994 to 2016 puts the digital share near 65.21 percent after ten years regardless of the start, unless the world body loses control, in which case the share collapses.
